problem: Prior VLN agents, whether trained models (Seq2Seq to DUET) or zero-shot LLM agents (NavGPT), use 'single-round self-thinking': one model receives all navigation information and must handle instruction parsing, perception, progress tracking and decision-making in a single inference. Even GPT-4 struggles with this. Sim-trained models also fail to transfer to real robots: DUET gets 0% SR on a real Turtlebot despite >70% SR in simulation.
motivation: Following an instruction step by step requires several distinct sub-skills: understanding action and landmark order, spotting instruction-relevant landmarks in 12 surrounding views, and estimating which sub-instructions are done. Each needs different knowledge. Inspired by human expert consultation meetings, the authors observe that large models' latent navigation abilities can be activated by role- and task-specific prompts. An agent that actively queries several specialized experts before each move can therefore reduce its reasoning burden, correct errors and filter inconsistent decisions, all without training.
key_idea: A GPT-4-driven zero-shot VLN agent (DiscussNav) that, before every step, 'discusses' with eight prompt-defined large-model domain experts (instruction analysis, vision perception, completion estimation, decision testing). It then samples N=5 chain-of-thought decisions, and a testing expert arbitrates when they disagree.
insight: Splitting the monolithic LLM decision into specialized, prompted sub-modules plus self-consistency-style arbitration helps a zero-shot agent a lot: SR rises from 34 to 43 and SPL from 29 to 40 over NavGPT on R2R val-unseen. The ablation (Table 2, 72-episode set) shows that vision perception experts (SR 32.46 without them) and completion estimation experts (SR 32.65 and the worst NE, 6.64, without them) matter most. Decision testing (SR 37.50 without) and instruction analysis (SR 38.77 without) help less. Tracking progress and asking landmark-type-targeted visual questions are therefore the key ingredients. The qualitative analysis adds two points: asking InstructBLIP type-targeted questions (e.g., 'What room / what color ... in direction k') reduces hallucination compared with NavGPT's generic 'A scene of' captioning prompt, and chaining experts lets later experts correct earlier errors, e.g., the landmark expert re-checking the action order.
method: Instruction analysis experts (GPT-4, T=0): an action decomposition expert splits the instruction into an ordered action sequence. A landmark extraction expert first error-checks that action order against the sentence structure, then extracts complete landmarks with their types (scene-level vs object-level, color, etc.). Both run once per episode.

Vision perception experts: each viewpoint is split into 12 directions of 30° FoV. A scene observation expert (InstructBLIP FlanT5-XL) is asked landmark-type-specific questions (e.g., 'What room can you see in the current direction {id}', 'What color of objects...') rather than questions about the existence of a concrete landmark, which reduces hallucination. An object detection expert (RAM-14M) returns object tags for each view.

Completion estimation experts: a trajectory summary expert (ChatGPT) compresses the navigation history into the format '[Step t] Observation: ... Thought: ...'. A completion estimation expert (GPT-4, chain-of-thought) checks passed landmarks and direction changes, then outputs Executed / In-progress / Waiting-to-be-executed actions.

DiscussNav decision agent (GPT-4, T=1, n=5 samples): fills question templates from a discussion corpus to query the experts. It then reasons via chain-of-thought (including a check that the completion estimate is correct) over landmarks, trajectory, completion state and 12-direction visual info, and emits N=5 'Prediction' directions. If all agree, it moves directly.

Decision testing experts: when the N predictions disagree, a thought fusion expert (ChatGPT) groups thought-prediction pairs by target and fuses their reasoning. A decision testing expert (GPT-4) then evaluates each option's feasibility against the current environment and selects the final move.

Execution: in the Matterport3D simulator the agent moves to the first candidate viewpoint in the predicted direction. On a Turtlebot 4 Lite it moves 0.5 m toward the predicted direction, or half the distance to an obstacle if one is within 1 m, with lidar used only for local obstacle avoidance.

numbers_note: Two caveats. (1) Table 1 uses '783 trajectories in the 11 val unseen environments' following NavGPT. That matches the number of R2R val-unseen paths, but it is unclear whether all 2349 instructions or one instruction per path were evaluated. (2) Table 2 (ablation) is stated to use a NavGPT-style 72-episode set (1 trajectory from each of 61 train + 11 val-unseen scenes). Yet its full DiscussNav row (9.69/5.32/61/43/40) is identical to Table 1's full val-unseen numbers, so the two tables' eval sets are inconsistent. The ablation variants, all on that 72-episode set, are: w/o Instruction Analysis SR 38.77 / SPL 35.04; w/o Vision Perception SR 32.46 / SPL 29.01; w/o Completion Estimation SR 32.65 / SPL 30.13 / NE 6.64; w/o Decision Testing SR 37.50 / SPL 33.31. The real-robot SR is measured on only 20 instructions.
results: On R2R val-unseen, DiscussNav reaches SR 43 / SPL 40 / NE 5.32 / OSR 61 / TL 9.69. It beats the previous zero-shot leader NavGPT (SR 34 / SPL 29), which the paper reports as a 26.47% relative SR gain and a 37.93% relative SPL gain, and it beats trained Seq2Seq and Speaker-Follower. It remains below trained EnvDrop (52/48) and pretrain-finetune models such as DUET (72/60). On a real Turtlebot 4 Lite with 20 instructions it gets 25% SR, versus NavGPT 10% and DUET 0%.
limitations: Very expensive per step: several GPT-4/ChatGPT calls, 5 sampled decisions and 12 InstructBLIP/RAM queries per viewpoint. Latency and cost are not reported, and the agent is still far below supervised VLN models in simulation.

Evaluation is thin and partly inconsistent: only R2R val-unseen (no test server, no other benchmarks). The ablation's claimed 72-episode set reuses the full-split numbers for the full model. The real-robot study covers only 20 instructions in one house.
Perception is reduced to text (captions/tags) from 12 fixed 30° views, so fine spatial and geometric information is lost. Hand-designed prompts and a fixed discussion order limit generality.
